questions.question: How do you use modules as mixins in Ruby?
questions.title: Modules as Mixins
questions.direct_answer: A module is a container of methods that you can mix into classes — giving Ruby a form of multiple inheritance. `module Walkable; def walk; 'walking'; end; end; class Dog; include Walkable; end; Dog.new.walk # 'walking'`. Include adds methods as instance methods; prepend inserts them ABOVE the class in lookup (so the module's method wins, can call super to the class); extend adds them as class methods. Mixins let you share behavior across unrelated classes (Dog and Cat both include Walkable, no shared parent). Use modules for cross-cutting behavior (Logging, Comparable, Enumerable) that doesn't model an is-a relationship. The ancestor chain reflects the order: include puts the module just above the includer; multiple includes stack in reverse. Prefer modules over deep inheritance for code reuse.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know modules mix behavior into classes (include = instance methods, extend = class methods) and why (multiple inheritance).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing include (instance) and extend (class), or expecting a module to be instantiated (modules can't be new'd).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Modules as mixins: include M -> instance methods; extend M -> class methods; prepend M -> above class. Share behavior across unrelated classes (multiple inheritance).

sections.title: Modules as Mixins
sections.content:
include=instance; extend=class; prepend=above. Share behavior across unrelated classes.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M[module Walkable] --> I[include -> instance methods]
  M --> E[extend -> class methods]
  M --> P[prepend -> above class]
  D[Dog + Walkable] --> Cat[Cat + Walkable, no shared parent]
```

sections.title: Modules as mixins
sections.content:
```ruby
module Walkable
  def walk; "#{self.class} is walking"; end
end

# include -> INSTANCE methods (mix into instances)
class Dog
  include Walkable
end
Dog.new.walk      # 'Dog is walking'  (instance method)
# Dog.walk        # NoMethodError (not a class method)

# extend -> CLASS methods
class Cat
  extend Walkable
end
Cat.walk          # 'Cat is walking'   (class method)
# Cat.new.walk    # NoMethodError (not an instance method)

# Share behavior across UNRELATED classes (no shared parent):
class Robot
  include Walkable
end
Robot.new.walk   # 'Robot is walking'  (Dog and Robot both walk)

class Car
  include Walkable
end
Car.new.walk     # 'Car is walking'   (4 classes, no common parent)

# prepend -> module method runs FIRST (above the class); can super to class
module Logged
  def save; puts 'saving'; super; end   # super -> the class's save
end
class Record
  prepend Logged
  def save; puts 'stored'; end
end
Record.new.save   # 'saving' then 'stored'  (module first, then class)
Record.ancestors  # [Logged, Record, Object, ...]  (module ABOVE class)

# Multiple includes stack in reverse order of inclusion:
class C; include A; include B; end   # ancestors: [B, A, C, ...]

# Modules CANNOT be instantiated: Walkable.new -> NoMethodError (no `new`).
# Use modules for CROSS-CUTTING behavior (Logging, Comparable, Enumerable).
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Confusing include (instance methods) and extend (class methods).
Expecting a module to be instantiated (modules can't be new'd).
Forgetting prepend puts the module ABOVE the class (its method wins).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A module is a container of methods mixed into classes (a form of multiple inheritance).
include M -> instance methods; extend M -> class methods; prepend M -> above the class.
Mixins share behavior across unrelated classes (Dog and Robot both include Walkable).
Use modules for cross-cutting behavior (Logging, Comparable, Enumerable) — not is-a.
Modules can't be instantiated (Walkable.new raises); multiple includes stack in reverse.
